title: Malaysia and Singapore
hookLine: long-settled Sikh communities with old gurdwaras

cards: Afternoon rain hammers a tin roof. Ceiling fans turn slowly over a hall of people sitting cross-legged on white sheets. A harmonium and a tabla carry a hymn over the noise of the storm.
Outside, frangipani trees drip, and a scooter splashes past. In the kitchen, rotis sit beside rice, because the cooks long ago learned what grows well here.
This is a gurdwara in Penang, or Kuala Lumpur, or Singapore, and the families in the hall don't think of it as a new arrival. Their grandparents prayed here.

teach.b: First, the arrival. Community histories tell of Sikh men who came to Malaya and Singapore in the days of British rule, to serve in the police and as guards and watchmen, and of others who came to trade or to farm cattle.
In time, wives and children followed, and a scattering of workers became a sangat. Second, the gurdwara.

teach.h: FIRST, A PLACE FOR THE GURU.
teach.b: Community histories tell how, once a few families had settled, a place for the Guru soon followed.

Some of those gurdwaras still stand, rebuilt and enlarged, with old photographs on the walls of men in turbans and uniforms. The gurdwara became the place for langar, Punjabi classes, weddings and help finding work.
Families here now count generations born in the tropics. Children grow up speaking English and the languages around them, and learn Punjabi in the gurdwara so they can read the Guru's words.
The weather changed, the food changed a little, the language around them changed. The hymns didn't. Fourth, the line underneath.
In a hymn by Guru Ram Das, at Ang 450 of the Guru Granth Sahib, the Guru says that wherever the True Guru goes and sits, that place becomes beautiful.
Some Sikhs hear in that a reason why no land is too far: where the Guru is seated and the sangat gathers, the place is made right.

how: Sikhs in Malaysia and Singapore keep long-established gurdwaras with daily kirtan, langar and Punjabi classes, and families mark gurpurabs and Vaisakhi there as Sikhs do elsewhere.

games.q: you've just settled in a hot, rainy town far from Punjab with a few other Sikh families. what do you build first?
o: nothing; you plan to go home soon.
games.why: community histories tell of a gurdwara going up early, and becoming the center of langar, classes and help.

practice: Picture yourself in that hall: rain on the tin roof, fans moving warm air, white sheets, the canopy, families in rows, old photographs on the wall.

Breathe in the smell of the kitchen, and on each breath out let the hymn carry over the storm. If you pray, you can say Waheguru the way the people in that hall might; if you don't, simply sit in the picture.

wordCard.voice: Gurdwara. The door of the Guru, whose old buildings in Malaysia and Singapore have held generations of Sikh families far from Punjab. Today's word.

orig.note: gurdwara, the door or house of the Guru; abroad, the first anchor of a sangat.

carryVoice: Your line: old roots abroad. A tree that grew where it was planted. See you tomorrow.
